components.text: Whether skepticism and evidence-based inquiry are incapable of addressing metaphysical or whole-reality questions.
The decisive demand is whether skepticism illegitimately excludes metaphysical inquiry merely by restricting itself to isolated empirical parts.
Whether the asserted essence-existence distinction and necessary being are adequately justified rather than inserted into the description.
The decisive demand is whether the essence-existence description justifies inferring a necessary being rather than merely stipulating necessity.
Whether an asserted absolute or simple ground is thereby identified with an agent, God, the Trinity, or classical theism.
Whether the observed world supplies evidence for the proposed absolute ground rather than merely motivating an open explanatory question.
The decisive demand is whether an asserted absolute ground discriminates an agent, God, or Trinity from non-agent and unknown alternatives.
A secondary demand is whether observed reality independently supports the asserted absolute ground in the first place.
Whether ordinary explanatory analogies provide independent support for essence, an act of existence, and a necessary metaphysical ground.
The decisive demand is whether ordinary causal analogy supplies comparable evidence for essence, existence itself, or a metaphysical ground.
A related demand is whether the inferred unity ground has empirical support comparable to familiar natural causal explanations.
Whether general terms such as human nature designate real essences rather than abstractions packaging physical beings and behavior.
The decisive demand is whether general nature-language identifies an objective constituent rather than packaging descriptions of physical beings.
Whether a purely descriptive account can explain personal identity and responsibility through ongoing material and temporal change.
The decisive demand is whether physical continuity and descriptive abstraction adequately explain personal identity through material change.
Whether conventional definitions merely create classifications or instead describe an objective nature belonging to the thing.
The decisive demand is whether conventional descriptions merely package experience or instead refer to an objective nature independent of words.
Whether identifying and describing an object requires an additional nonphysical essence beyond physical properties, function, and learned concepts.
Whether the pen example answers the separate problem of diachronic personal persistence through material change.
The decisive demand is whether word-independent recognition of a pen establishes a further nonphysical essence beyond its properties and function.
A related demand is whether identification and continuity require an additional form rather than tracked physical and functional features.
Whether composition or multiplicity itself licenses an inference to intentional assembly or an external composing agent.
The decisive demand is whether composition itself warrants an intentional composer rather than only some explanation of organization.
Whether the universe's composition supplies a general basis for inferring an external composer despite the artifact-natural disanalogy.
The decisive demand is whether natural composition has independent evidence of intentional assembly comparable to known artifacts.
Whether composition independently establishes an intentional composer rather than presupposing that all parts-bearing things are agent-assembled.
The decisive demand is whether parts independently imply an intentional composer rather than assuming the universal agency premise.
Whether the transition from finite or accidental existence to a per-se self-existent ground has an articulated logical principle.
Whether a self-declared metaphysical principle supplies the independent evidential warrant missing from the burnt-wood analogy.
The decisive demand is whether the necessity bridge is independently justified rather than introduced through unsupported terminology.
Whether purported divine revelation has publicly assessable indicators beyond private conviction or ambiguous personal experience.
Whether historical revelation could provide the additional evidence needed to identify an abstract ground with a revealed God.
The decisive demand is whether purported revelation supplies publicly assessable evidence despite sincere nonbelief and unclear disclosure.
Whether the inference to the Christian God has adequate independently supported and discriminating evidence given its background plausibility.
Whether philosophical reasoning supplies the missing identity bridge from necessary creator to the specifically Christian God.
Whether empirical examination of parts is methodologically sufficient for questions about reality as a whole.
The decisive demand is whether the Christian-God inference has adequate independent and background evidence proportionate to its claim.
A secondary demand is whether nonempirical whole-level inquiry can meet sound truth-seeking and evidential standards.
